# Diagnosing AC Squeals on a 1990 Winnebago: A Mechanical Diagnosis

A loud squeal that intensifies when turning the steering wheel on a 1990 G30 chassis Winnebago points to a specific mechanical coupling between the air conditioning system and the power steering pump. The fact that you replaced the AC compressor without resolving the issue suggests the root cause lies in the accessory drive belt path or the tensioner mechanism, rather than the internal state of the new compressor itself.

On vehicles equipped with the 454 V8 engine found in these chassis, the serpentine or V-belt system often shares a single drive belt that powers both the alternator, water pump, and the accessories for the AC and power steering. When you turn the wheel, the power steering pump requires significantly more torque to assist with steering effort. If this load spike causes a belt slip, it generates high-frequency squealing. The persistence of the noise even after swapping the compressor indicates that the belt is likely worn, glazed, or insufficiently tensioned to handle the combined load of the AC clutch engaging and the power steering pump assisting simultaneously.

Inspecting the belt for signs of glazing is the first logical step. A belt that has been slipping under previous loads will develop a shiny, smooth surface on the ribbed side, losing its ability to grip the pulleys effectively. You should also check for missing ribs or cracks in the rubber material. If the belt looks intact but the noise persists, the issue almost certainly resides with the belt tensioner. On many GM-based chassis from this era, the automatic tensioner fails over time due to seized bearings or weak internal springs. When the AC clutch engages, it adds a radial load to the system. If the tensioner cannot maintain adequate clamping force during this transition, the belt slips against the idler pulley or the power steering pump pulley.

The chirping noise heard when the AC is off is less alarming but still indicative of friction issues. This could be an idler pulley bearing that is failing to spin freely. When the system is under load from the AC clutch, the bearing may seize momentarily or create enough drag to cause slippage. You can verify this by manually spinning each pulley in the belt path while the engine is off. Any pulley that does not rotate with absolute smoothness or returns to a stopped position after you give it a flick should be replaced immediately.

Replacing the tensioner and idler pulleys is often a more cost-effective solution than assuming the new compressor is defective, provided the compressor shaft spins freely. If the noise continues after addressing the belt path, check the alignment of all pulleys. Misaligned pulleys create uneven belt wear and increased friction, leading to squeals under load. A visual inspection with the hood open usually reveals a flat spot or "step" in the belt path if alignment is off.

Finally, ensure the AC clutch engagement solenoid is functioning correctly. If the clutch engages while the compressor shaft is not yet spinning at full speed due to internal drag (even in a new unit, though rare), the sudden load can cause a slip event. However, given the steering correlation, the belt path remains the primary suspect until proven otherwise. Addressing the tensioner and belt condition should eliminate both the squeal under steering input and the intermittent chirp when the system is idle.
